patient.chief_complaint: Five-day rapidly progressive ascending leg weakness and areflexia with bilateral facial diplegia, preceded by Campylobacter gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago. Unable to walk. Respiratory function declining.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W. is a 35-year-old physical therapist presenting with a 5-day history of rapidly progressive neurological symptoms. Two weeks before admission, he had confirmed Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis (stool culture positive at an urgent care clinic) lasting 4 days. He recovered but 10 days later developed bilateral foot tingling. Over the following 5 days, weakness ascended rapidly from his feet to his hips. He is now unable to walk. Yesterday he noticed bilateral facial drooping and slurred speech. He has had dysphagia for thin liquids since this morning. As a physical therapist, he recognized the pattern immediately and came to the ED. FVC on arrival is 1.8 L (43% predicted). He is alarmed and asking for IVIG. He has no bowel or bladder symptoms. No neck stiffness. No fever since his gastroenteritis resolved.

specialized_test.impression: Severe acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP). Fulfills all electrodiagnostic criteria for GBS. Markedly prolonged distal motor latencies, severely reduced conduction velocities, absent F-waves and H-reflex, absent sensory SNAPs bilaterally. Classic albumino-cytologic dissociation pattern expected.

optimal_actions.action: Immediate respiratory assessment — FVC and NIF

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Severe AIDP meeting all electrophysiological criteria

optimal_actions.action: Labs including Campylobacter serology, inflammatory markers

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus tachycardia, QTc prolongation, autonomic dysrhythmias

critical_actions: INTUBATE NOW — FVC 18 mL/kg (<20 mL/kg threshold), NIF -22, CO2 rising
Do NOT delay intubation — elective RSI before crisis is essential
ICU admission with continuous telemetry — severe autonomic instability expected
contraindicated_actions: Corticosteroids — absolutely no benefit; do not give
Combining IVIG and plasmapheresis simultaneously — no additive benefit
Succinylcholine for RSI intubation in GBS — risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia due to upregulated acetylcholine receptors; use rocuronium instead
key_reasoning_points: Classic GBS: ascending paralysis + areflexia + bilateral facial diplegia + preceding C. jejuni infection + albumino-cytologic dissociation = textbook AIDP
SUCCINYLCHOLINE IS CONTRAINDICATED for RSI in GBS — use rocuronium; succinylcholine can cause fatal hyperkalemia in GBS due to upregulated nicotinic receptors
High-titer anti-GM1/GD1a IgG predicts risk of secondary axonal injury and slower recovery
Severe autonomic instability (life-threatening bradycardia, hypertensive and hypotensive crises) is a major GBS complication requiring ICU management
This patient is a physical therapist who recognized GBS — but even expert recognition does not change the management imperatives
